items.content: Objective. To evaluate the effectiveness of Tuina-focused integrative Chinese medical therapies (TICMT) on inpatients with low back pain (LBP). Methods. 6 English and Chinese databases were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of TICMT for in-patients with LBP. The methodological quality of the included RCTs was assessed based on PEDro scale. And the meta-analyses of TICMT for LBP on pain and functional status were conducted. Results. 20 RCTs were included. The methodological quality of the included RCTs was poor. The meta-analyses' results showed that TICMT had statistically significant effects on pain and functional status, especially Tuina plus Chinese herbal medicine (standardised mean difference, SMD: 1.17; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.60 on pain; SMD: 1.31; 95% CI 0.49 to 2.14 on functional status) and Tuina plus acupuncture (SMD: 0.94; 95% CI 0.38 to 1.50 on pain; SMD: 0.53; 95% CI 0.21 to 0.85 on functional status). But Tuina plus moxibustion or hot pack did not show significant improvements on pain. And the long-term evidence of TICMT was far from sufficient. Conclusions. The preliminary evidence from current studies suggests that TICMT might be effective complementary and alternative treatments for in-patients with LBP. However, the poor methodological quality of the included RCTs means that high-quality RCTs with long follow-up are warranted.

items.content:
CRD summary
The review concluded that there was insufficient evidence to show that Guasha was effective in treating musculoskeletal pain. There were some potential weaknesses in the review methodology and the evidence was limited and of poor quality, therefore the authors’ cautious conclusions are likely to be reliable.
Authors' objectives
To evaluate the effectiveness of Guasha in treating musculoskeletal pain.
Searching
The following databases were searched to July 2009 for publications in any language: MEDLINE (from 1969), AMED (from 1995), EMBASE (from 1966), CINAHL (from 1981), DBPIA/DBpia (from 1966), KISS (from 1966), KISTI (from 1959), KoreaMed (from 1959), RISS (from 1959), CNKI (from 1974), and the Cochrane Library. Search terms were reported. The journals, Focus on Alternative and Complementary Therapies plus Research in Complementary Medicine, were also searched from 1994 to July 2009. Bibliographies of each retrieved article and also some relevant articles in the authors’ department were handsearched.
Study selection
Controlled clinical trials (CCTs) that evaluated Guasha (a therapeutic method of pain management using tools to scrape or rub the surface of the body to relieve blood stagnation) in the treatment of patients diagnosed with musculoskeletal pain (regardless of age or gender) were eligible for inclusion. Trials were excluded if they compared one type of Guasha with another, or if Guasha was a part of a complex intervention. Relevant outcomes were not specified.
All the included trials were conducted in China. The Guasha session time length in the interventions was 20 minutes (reported only in a few trials), given every two to seven days, with a total of three to 10 sessions (where reported). The most common comparative intervention was acupuncture; others were acupuncture plus moxibustion, massage, electric current therapy, herbal injections, or no treatment (details were given). Several trials were of patients with cervical spondylosis; the other trials included patients with fibromyalgia, neck stiffness, scapulohumeral periarthritis, or lumbar disc herniation. The outcomes reported in the included trials were response rate, the number of pain points, pain on a visual analogue scale (VAS), and adverse events.
Two independent reviewers performed the selection.
Assessment of study quality
Four Cochrane criteria were used to assess quality: sequence generation, blinding, incomplete outcome measures, and allocation concealment. Blinding of patient/assessor was assessed separately.
Methodological quality was assessed by two reviewers independently, with disagreements resolved by discussion and, when necessary, by consulting a third reviewer.
Data extraction
Response rates were extracted, which was divided initially into four categories: recovery, marked improvement, improvement, and no change; but response rates were only calculated for recovery and improvement. Relative risk (RR) or mean difference (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for each trial.
Data extraction was performed by two reviewers independently, with disagreements resolved by discussion and, when necessary, by consulting a third reviewer.
Methods of synthesis
A narrative synthesis was provided.
Results of the review
Seven studies were identified (n=736 patients; range 50 to 240), including five randomised controlled trials (RCTs; n=420 patients; range 50 to 120) and two CCTs (n=316 patients; 76 and 240). All the trials were reported to suffer from performance bias, attrition bias and detection bias; none reported randomisation method, allocation concealment, the blinding of outcome assessors, drop-outs or withdrawals.
Only one of seven trials reported an increase in improvement rate for Guasha compared with control treatments (RR 1.3, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.13), but the data provided did not appear to be significant. This RCT included patients with fibromyalgia and found a significant decrease in the number of pain points (MD -5.0, 95% CI -6.5 to -3.5) and pain measured using a VAS with a maximum of 100mm (MD -9.5, 95% CI -14.5 to -4.5) for Guasha versus acupuncture treatment.
Three of six trials found a significant increase in recovery rate for Guasha compared with control treatments. All three studies compared Guasha with acupuncture: an RCT of patients with fibromyalgia (RR 2.9, 95% CI 1.55 to 5.41); an RCT of patients with scapulohumeral periarthritis (RR 1.8, 95% CI 1.00 to 3.25); and a CCT of patients with cervical spondylosis (RR 1.53, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.20).
No adverse events were reported for any of the seven trials.
Authors' conclusions
Currently available evidence was insufficient to show that Guasha was effective in pain management. Further RCTs are warranted and methodological quality should be improved.
CRD commentary
The review addressed a well-defined question in terms of participants, interventions and study design; the criteria were broad for outcomes. Relevant databases were searched in any language. Publication bias was not assessed. Efforts were made to reduce error and bias throughout the review process.
Trial quality was assessed using suitable criteria and some relevant data was provided. Some relevant trial details were reported, but no details of length of follow-up or loss to follow-up were given, or the age and gender of patients. Statistical heterogeneity was not assessed. A narrative synthesis was presented presumably because of the heterogeneity of the trials. The outcomes and analysis performed for the individual trials was not clearly described. The authors reported that one trial result was statistically significant when it did not appear to be so. The included trials were generally of poor quality.
The authors reported that the evidence was insufficient and of low quality and that there was potential for publication bias; their cautious conclusions are likely to be reliable.
Implications of the review for practice and research
Practice
: The authors did not state any implications for practice.
Research
: The authors identified a need for further RCTs which use high standards of trial methodology, with sufficient sample sizes, validated outcome measurement and an adequate placebo procedure. Future studies should also consider the combined use of Guasha with other therapies.
Funding
Korea Institute of Oriental Medicine.
